articleHeadline: Meningitis Cases in Ghana
articleSummary: Ghana continues to grapple with meningitis, predominantly in the Northern, Upper East and Upper West Regions, where the disease is endemic and outbreaks occur mainly during the dry season (November–April). From 1998–2021 there were over 71,000 suspected cases and about 3,865 confirmed cases; case fatality historically ranges from 20% to 47%, with some outbreaks reaching 36%–50%. In 2025, the Upper West Region reported about 269 suspected cases and 36 confirmed cases with several deaths; the Upper East Region had 31 suspected cases with confirmed deaths. Seasonal surveillance January–March shows rising case numbers. High-prevalence districts reach up to 54%, while Greater Accra and Ashanti remain low (often <5%). Most cases are bacterial meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae. Those most affected are children and young adults (5–29); males slightly more than females. Vaccination (e.g., MenAfriVac), surveillance, and prompt antibiotic treatment reduce deaths.
notes: ガーナは髄膜炎の風土病地域であり、乾季（11月-4月）に流行する典型的なパターンを示している。2025年の上西部地域での269疑似症例・36確認症例、上東部地域での31疑似症例と死亡の報告は、季節性監視下での上昇傾向を示唆している。主要病原体はStreptococcus pneumoniae、Neisseria meningitidis、Haemophilus influenzaeである。5-29歳の小児・若年成人が最も影響を受けており、ワクチン（MenAfriVac）の接種率・抗生物質への早期アクセス・監視体制が重要な課題と考えられる。

articleHeadline: LRP8 is a functional receptor for yellow fever virus - Nature Microbiology
articleSummary: LRP8 (ApoER2) functions as a receptor for yellow fever virus (YFV). In a genome-wide barcoded ORFeome overexpression screen in HEK293T cells, LRP8 ranked among top enrichment for GFP-positive YFV-infected cells, implicating it as an entry factor. LRP8 overexpression markedly increased infection by YFV‑17D pseudoviruses and by live YFV BJ01 (Angola genotype; derived from a rare China spillover case) but not Zika virus. An antibody against the extracellular domain blocked YFV but not Zika, supporting a cell-surface receptor role. Binding and internalization assays showed LRP8 enhances YFV attachment and uptake, while KO reduces them. Other tested flavivirus pseudotypes showed no LRP8 dependence, indicating YFV specificity.

Local authorities initiated contact tracing and provided antibiotic prophylaxis or vaccination to dozens of close contacts in home, school, and health facilities; environmental disinfection and public education on early signs and hygiene were conducted. articleSummary: HFMD cases in Vietnam show a sharp rise; nearly 3,000 infections at the National Children's Hospital in the first two months of 2026; HFMD cases up 56% compared with the same period in 2025, and hospitalizations have doubled. Most affected are children under five; the disease is caused by enteroviruses and spreads via the digestive tract. While usually mild, serious complications such as encephalitis, meningitis, myocarditis, and acute pulmonary edema can occur and be fatal if not treated promptly. Re-infections are possible since immunity to one strain (Coxsackie, EV71) does not protect against others; the number of skin lesions does not indicate severity. Warning signs needing urgent care include persistent high fever over 39 C unresponsive to meds, sudden repetitive tremors or spasms, especially when falling asleep, and unsteady movements. Do not give antibiotics; maintain good hygiene, wash with clean water or antiseptic soap, do not puncture blisters, and trim nails to prevent scratching and secondary infection.

articleSummary: Leptospirosis outbreaks in Peru, with three deaths in Piura, San Martín, and Tumbes, amid rising cases linked to humidity and floods. Highest incidence is in Loreto, Madre de Dios, Tumbes, Ucayali, San Martín, Amazonas, Ayacucho, Huánuco, and Cusco, with the Health Ministry intensifying response. The National Institute of Health conducts quality controls, distributes 500 ELISA IgM kits, and promotes molecular testing, while training over 300 professionals in surveillance, diagnosis, and clinical management; cases are followed up and community surveillance committees formed. Transmission occurs via contact with water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals, primarily rodents. Symptoms include fever, lower back and leg pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and red eyes. Prevention: avoid stagnant water, wear protective boots in flooded areas, practice hand hygiene, wash foods, and boil water. Seek care promptly; do not self-medicate.
